human reviewers only identified 68% of research abstracts created by ChatGPT.
Applied linguists have done rather better at distinguishing machine-generated texts from those
written by humans. A growing body of research has begun to show that ChatGPT does not write like
humans in terms of linguistic features, rhetorical strategies, or even content (Yang et al., 2024). Indeed,
in one comparative study, Herbold et al. (2023) found that expert markers rated ChatGPT generated
essays more highly than those produced by German high school students, with the AI models exhibit-
ing linguistic characteristics distinct from those of the human-written essays. Similarly, Kong and Liu
(2024) also found significant differences between human and AI-generated texts. Examining research
[TEXT OMITTED FROM FIXTURE].
result of genetic engineering.
(Student essay)
In contrast, ChatGPT essays contained very few questions. Instead, the model prioritises clarity and
structural coherence, reflecting its algorithmic nature and training. So, while ChatGPT can generate
reasoned and contextually appropriate text, it lacks an inherent understanding of audience. Unlike
human writers, who develop a mental model of their readers and adjust their writing accordingly
(Hyland & Jiang, 2023), ChatGPT does not possess an intrinsic awareness of who might be reading
its output. Similarly, M. Zhang & Crosthwaite (2025) found that ChatGPT excels in generating texts
with formal and complex vocabulary suited for academic and technical themes, while undergraduate
L2 writers focused on personal and social issues, using more varied and context-rich vocabulary.
This gap between informational load and reader engagement is also shown in the grammar of
texts created by the two sources. Research shows that AI generated texts exhibit higher density of
content with more noun and preposition-based structures (Herbold et al., 2023; Markey et al., 2024),
while human-authored texts contained more clause-related bundles and use of stance markers (Jiang
& Hyland, 2024). Markey et al. (2024), for instance, analysed a small corpus of AI generated texts
in two genres and compared them with novice and published academic writers, observing that the
ChatGPT texts were more informationally dense than authored texts and often read as dialogically
[TEXT OMITTED FROM FIXTURE].
many teachers would encourage in their students. But we are usually not encouraging students to
write in the style of research papers but in ways that effectively engage with and persuade teachers,
supervisors and peers. Texts created by ChatGPT’s statistical algorithms therefore appear to be ‘vaguer
and more formulaic’ (Gao et al., 2023, p. 1), reinforcing a reductionist view of writing where it might
be seen as a fixed structure following a system of grammatical rules (Vee, 2023). Because it tends
to objectivise academic writing it ‘fails to take account of the beliefs and knowledge writers assume
readers will draw on in reading their texts’ (Hyland, 2026, p. 6). Other evidence supports this view.
Yang et al. (2024), for example, found that ChatGPT texts rely more on repetitive connective signals
and constant thematic progression, suggesting less careful planning for text development, which leads
to redundancy and a simplistic list-like structure.
So, if GPT can’t write papers like students, then it does not have the resources to offer useful feed-
back. How can it evaluate, correct and advise students on their argumentative writing? As Jiang and
Hyland (Jiang & Hyland, 2025b, p. 26) observe:
The limited use of these strategies in ChatGPT texts suggests a missed opportunity for enhanc-
ing reader engagement and interaction, which could contribute to more natural, human-like,
and persuasive discourse. This points once again to the model’s training parameters, which
seem to prioritize informational flow and the conventions of academic formality over interac-
tive discourse that create reader engagement.
The problem is that AI users, whether students or teachers, cannot determine the source texts which
comprise its training data. While users can now add plug-ins to bring their relevant data into the
chatbot to train ChatGPT, this is only available to the subscription version ChatGPT Plus, which many
teachers are unlikely to have access to. The use of third-party builders like BotSonic or SocialIntents to
train a custom chatbot may also be beyond the reach of most teachers. Without these workarounds,
we can’t be sure that the output produced by Gen AI is truly representative of writing in the target
[TEXT OMITTED FROM FIXTURE].
In other words, the Gen AI feedback seems formulaic while positive feedback lacks sincerity and
specificity.
4. Is it trusted and valued by learners?
Much of the available research focuses on the personalised nature of the feedback that AI can instantly
provide. But does this swing students towards a preference for AI feedback?
Li et al. (2024) found both GPT3.5 and GPT4o’s written feedback was highly rated by Chinese
tertiary L2 English students as being more relevant to their specific needs as compared with teach-
ers’ more general feedback. A systematic review of 52 studies of AWE feedback found that students
generally considered automated feedback useful and were motivated when using it, although they
criticised a lack of accuracy and explicitness as the feedback tended to be generic and formulaic (Fu
et al., 2022). In addition, teachers’ feedback focused mainly on accuracy and was seen as less relevant
regarding content and organisation, while GPT’s feedback was considered as balanced across each
domain. Chan et al’s randomised controlled trial (Chan et al., 2024) with Hong Kong students arrived
at similar findings. The researchers concluded that the group who received AI feedback demonstrated
statistically significant improvements in the quality of their writing compared with those receiving
teacher feedback, and they also reported higher levels of motivation and engagement during revising.
Escalante et al. (2023) found an equal split among students voting for AI-generated versus human-
generated feedback after a six-week course with weekly feedback from both on short assignments.
The main reason for preferring tutor feedback was that interacting face to face with a human was
seen to be ‘more engaging’ compared to reading through AI-generated feedback. They liked the way
they could ask follow-up questions and get immediate feedback while allowing them to develop their
writing and speaking skills at the same time.
Those students preferring AI-generated feedback cited the clarity, understandability, consistency,
[TEXT OMITTED FROM FIXTURE].
ability to recognise the value of the advice they receive? Can they incorporate it into their repertoire,
transferring the skills to improve and apply the knowledge in later contexts? This implies developing
critical thinking, enhancing metacognitive awareness, and fostering self-regulated learning.
In an experimental study comparing student writing over a six-week course Escalante et al. (2023)
found no difference in learning outcomes between a group receiving AI feedback and one receiving
human tutor feedback. While studies have generally found AI to have a positive effect on writing
development, particularly if they lead to substantive revisions (Roscoe et al., 2017), some report
inconsistent improvements (see Zhai & Ma, 2023). For example, Stevenson and Phakiti (2019) found
that L2 students using AWE reduced error rates across drafts of the same task, but that learning did
not transfer across tasks.
We have noted that AI feedback is especially good at:
• Spotting grammar and spelling errors

• Suggesting sentence rephrasing

But while this kind of surface-level correction can help improve the current draft, it is unlikely
to lead to long-term learning unless the student reflects on and understands the feedback. Effective
prompts and continuing dialogues with GenAI seem important. Some studies show that when stu-
dents engage actively with AI feedback (e.g. using it to revise, reflect on errors, compare drafts,
and so on), they improve not just their texts but their language and writing skills. However, passive
use – just accepting changes without understanding them – tends to only improve only the current
text, not the student.
Fuchs (2023), for example, warns that students’ uncritical acceptance of Gen AI feedback may
mean they fail to develop academic skills such as evaluating sources for quality and reliability. One
aspect of improving writers’ skills is the development of their autonomy, but it is unclear how far it
does so. A meta-analysis of 18 peer-reviewed articles on AI feedback by Mohebbi (2025), for example,
found that AI promoted self-regulated learning but flagged the dangers of an over-reliance on tech-
nology, potentially hindering their development of critical writing and editing skills (Kohnke et al.,
2023). So, specific challenges arising from students’ over-reliance on Gen AI are that it could reduce
their creativeness, criticality, clarity, and linguistic precision, each of which are key skills allowing
them to connect their real-world experiences to their academic writing (Creely, 2024; Crompton et al.,
2024). In sum, Gen AI may deprive students of learning opportunities and hinder the development
of an academic voice (Barrot, 2023; Park & Ahn, 2024).
The central problem, I think, is that we are still at the gee whizz stage of AI development where
[TEXT OMITTED FROM FIXTURE].
Students get AI feedback and then categorise their errors (e.g. tenses, word order, lexical
choices). Over time, they build an awareness of language and their writing weaknesses.
3. AI as a writing coach
With improved digital literacy among teachers it may be possible to set up ChatGPT as a coach
students can query about improving clarity, structure, or argumentation in their essays. This
interactive format helps students think metacognitively.
Adopting such a collaborative model, Han and Li (2024) asked over 100 students to complete two
writing tasks, with both corrective and holistic feedback provided by ChatGPT which was later mod-
ified by teachers for students’ subsequent use. Results suggest the students incorporated more of this
co-produced feedback into subsequent revisions, in effect ‘leveraging the analytic strengths of AI
while maintaining essential teacher-student interactions’ (p. 1). We cannot, then, be taken in a direc-
tion led by the technology and the megacorporations behind it. Teachers do not want to be replaced
by AI, and outcomes are better when they are not. At the core of this balanced approach is foster-
ing student agency and critical AI literacy – the ability to use AI effectively while understanding its
limitations and biases.

1. Plenary given at the WCF25 Conference, held on 5th and 6th of June 2025 at the Autonomous University of Barcelona.
